transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I guess what brings me in is that I just keep dodging anything that even smells like my old job. I was an operations manager for years, and honestly, the commute alone was always such a nightmare. I used to drive down Route 4, and they've been doing construction there for what feels like a decade. My husband always told me to take the back roads, but those roads have terrible potholes that just ruin your suspension, and getting a mechanic you trust these days is nearly impossible... anyway, what was I saying? 

Right, the job. I just can't go near office buildings anymore. Or sit through security talks, or go to those networking events near the work sites. Which, to be honest, networking is exhausting anyway. You just stand around holding a tiny plate of dry cheese, trying to look interested in someone's supply chain issues. I'd much rather be home working on my garden. My hydrangeas are actually doing so well this year, I finally got the soil acidity right. 

But yeah... if anyone at those things, or anywhere really, starts asking about the day it happened... I just make some excuse and get out. I just have to leave.
What happened on the day you're referring to that makes you want to leave when people ask about it?

I... I really don't know how to explain what happened. I just can't get into it. It's... it's just too much. So I just grab my things and head straight out to the car. 

I actually just had to get new tires on my car, which was a whole ordeal in itself. You go in for a simple oil change and suddenly they're telling you the tread is worn down to nothing and it's a safety hazard. I mean, I know you need good tires, especially with all the rain we've been having lately. The ground is just saturated. My basement almost flooded last week because the gutters were backed up. My husband was supposed to clean them out back in October, but he tweaked his lower back playing pickleball. Have you noticed that? Everyone is playing pickleball now! It's like it took over the whole neighborhood overnight. They even repurposed the old tennis courts at the park down the street, and now you hear that popping sound all day long if you leave the windows open... 

But anyway, what did you ask me? Oh, right. The day. Yeah, I just... I can't really talk about it. I just have to leave when it comes up.
Do you ever have episodes where you suddenly feel intense fear or discomfort that reaches a peak within minutes?

Intense fear out of nowhere? No, I don't think I get anything like that. I mean, I get stressed, sure, but not like a sudden peak of panic or whatever. Actually, the most stressed I've been lately was when I was trying to get my mother's Medicare sorted out. Have you ever tried calling them? You sit on hold for forty-five minutes listening to that awful elevator music. And it's not even good elevator music, it's like a synthesizer from 1985 just playing the same four chords over and over. I was on the phone with them while I was trying to bake a lasagna, and I completely lost track of time. Burnt the edges to a crisp. My husband said he likes it crispy, but he was just being nice. He's sweet like that, mostly. We've been married thirty-two years next month. We were thinking about going to Cape Cod for our anniversary, but the rentals have gotten so expensive. A little two-bedroom cottage is practically the price of a mortgage payment now. It's ridiculous. 

But no, to answer your question, I don't really have those sudden fear episodes. Just the regular kind of stress, you know?
Do you find yourself avoiding people, places, or activities because they remind you of something unpleasant?

Well, yes, I think I mentioned that earlier. I just keep dodging anything that even smells like my old job. Office buildings, those security talks, networking events near the work sites... I just avoid them all completely. And like I said, if anyone starts asking about the day it happened, I just make up an excuse and get out of there. 

Actually, speaking of making excuses, I had to do that just last week at my book club. We were supposed to be reading that new historical fiction novel—the one with the blue cover? Everyone's talking about it. But I just couldn't get into it. The main character was so whiny, honestly. So I told them I had a migraine and left early. I felt a little bad, but Mary was making her famous artichoke dip, and she always uses way too much garlic. I mean, I love garlic, but you don't need three whole cloves for one little bowl of dip. My husband couldn't even stand to be in the same room as me the last time I ate it. We had to sleep with the window cracked, and it was freezing out! The heating bill this month was already astronomical because they raised the rates again. It's like everything just keeps going up... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, avoiding things. Yeah, I definitely avoid anything to do with that job or that day. I just can't do it.
Do you ever have memories or thoughts about what happened on that day that come into your mind when you don't want them to?

Well, yeah, that happens a lot, actually. Out of nowhere I'll be washing the dishes, or, you know, just driving past a warehouse gate, and suddenly the whole scene just pops right back into my head. It's so sharp, I can hear the panic in people's voices, and my chest tightens up like I'm right back there. It's awful. 

I was actually washing dishes just yesterday when it happened. I was using that new lemon-scented soap. Have you tried it? It's supposed to cut through grease better, but honestly, it just leaves a weird film on the glassware. I had to rewash all my wine glasses before my sister came over. She's so particular about things like that. She was coming over to help me pick out new curtains for the living room, but we ended up just arguing about the color. She thinks I should go with a sage green, but I'm leaning more towards a dusty rose. The couch is already a neutral beige, so I feel like we need a pop of color, you know? Plus, the dog sheds so much, and beige just hides the fur better. He's a Golden Retriever mix, sweetest thing, but the shedding is out of control. I have to vacuum every single day, and my vacuum is on its last legs. It makes this horrible screeching noise when I push it over the rug... 

But anyway, yeah, the memories. They just come out of nowhere, and it feels like I'm right back in it.
How long have you been avoiding things that remind you of your old job?

Well, it's been going on since I was fired after that whole armed incident. So, about a year and seven months ago, I'd say. I remember because it was right around the time I decided to finally redo the downstairs bathroom. We had this awful, peeling floral wallpaper from the nineties—just these huge, garish pink peonies everywhere. I spent three whole weekends steaming and scraping that stuff off the walls. My shoulders ached for a month! And then, of course, once the wallpaper was gone, the old vanity looked terrible, so we had to replace that too. We went to one of those big box hardware stores, and you wouldn't believe how hard it is to find a simple, white vanity that doesn't cost an arm and a leg. The guy working in the plumbing aisle was absolutely no help either. He just kept pointing me toward these modern, floating sink things. I told him, "I have a thirty-two-year-old house, a floating sink is going to look ridiculous." We ended up just ordering one online, but the delivery got delayed twice because of some storm back east... 

But yes, to answer your question, it's been about a year and seven months of avoiding all that stuff from work.
Do you feel any physical sensations, like a racing heart or sweating, when those memories of what happened on that day come into your mind?

Well, I don't really know about physical things. I haven't really noticed my heart racing or sweating or anything like that. When the memories come, it's just... it's just the memory, you know? It's not like I'm breaking out in a sweat or anything. 

Speaking of sweating, though, this hot flash thing I've been dealing with lately is just ridiculous. I mean, I'll be sitting perfectly still, reading a magazine, and suddenly I'm just drenched. It's so uncomfortable. I had to buy these special cooling sheets for the bed, which cost a fortune, by the way. And my husband, he's always cold, so he's sleeping under two blankets while I've got the fan pointed right at my face. He actually complained the other night that the fan was too loud. I told him, "Well, it's either the fan or I melt into a puddle, so pick one." He ended up sleeping in the guest room, which is fine by me because he snores anyway. Not a little snore, either, it's like a freight train. I've told him a hundred times he needs to get one of those sleep studies done, but he won't listen. He says it's just allergies. But allergies don't make you sound like a chainsaw, do they? 

So, yeah, no racing heart or sweating from the memories. Just the regular kind of sweating.
Do you feel distressed when those memories of what happened on that day come into your mind?

Well, no, not really. I don't feel distressed or anything when they pop up. It's just the memory playing in my head, you know? It doesn't make me upset or anything like that.

But speaking of being upset, I was just furious at the grocery store the other day. I go to the one on Elm Street because they usually have the best produce, but lately, it's just been awful. I was looking for a decent head of lettuce, and every single one was bruised or wilted. I mean, they charge three dollars for a head of lettuce now, and it looks like it's been kicked across the floor! I asked the kid stocking the carrots if they had any fresh ones in the back, and he just shrugged at me. Didn't even go check! Just shrugged and went back to his phone. Kids these days have absolutely no work ethic. When I was his age, working my first job at the diner, if a customer asked for something, you ran to get it. You didn't just stand there texting. And don't even get me started on the self-checkout lines. They installed six new ones and only have one actual cashier working. I had a whole cart full of groceries, and the machine kept yelling at me about an "unexpected item in the bagging area." It was just my purse! I had to wait ten minutes for someone to come over and clear the error. 

But anyway, no, the memories don't really bother me or make me feel distressed.
Are there any specific things you avoid because they remind you of what happened on that day?

Well, yeah, actually. I keep dodging anything that even smells like that old job. Like, office buildings, those security talks they used to make us do, or even networking events near the work sites. And if people start asking about the day it happened, I just make some excuse and get out of there. 

Which reminds me, I had to make an excuse to get out of my neighbor Susan's Tupperware party last week. I mean, who even sells Tupperware anymore? I thought that went out in the eighties. But she had this whole spread laid out—little cucumber sandwiches and those meatballs in the grape jelly sauce. Have you ever had those? They sound disgusting, but they're actually pretty good. Anyway, she cornered me by the dip and started showing me this modular mate system for the pantry. I have a perfectly fine system in my pantry, thank you very much. I use those glass jars with the clamp lids. They look so much nicer than plastic, and they don't stain when you put tomato sauce in them. I bought a set of plastic containers once, and after one round of leftover spaghetti, they were permanently orange. It's impossible to get that out. I tried baking soda, vinegar, leaving them in the sun... nothing worked. So I just threw them all in the recycling bin. I read an article recently that said most of what we put in the recycling doesn't even get recycled anyway. It just ends up in a landfill or shipped off to some other country. It really makes you wonder why we bother washing all out the peanut butter jars if they're just going to throw them in the trash. 

But yeah, anyway, I avoid all those work-related things and definitely get out of there if people bring up that day.
Do you try to push away or avoid thoughts or memories about what happened on that day when they come into your mind?

Well, yeah, like I was just saying, I try to push it all away. I keep dodging anything that even smells like that old job. Office buildings, those security talks, networking events near the work sites... and if people start asking about the day it happened, I just make some excuse and get out. 

I'm actually getting pretty good at making excuses. The other day, I told the mailman I had something burning on the stove just so I wouldn't have to talk to him. He's a nice enough guy, I guess, but he always wants to chat about the weather or his dog's hip dysplasia. I mean, I feel bad for the dog, but what am I supposed to do about it? I'm not a vet. My sister had a golden retriever with bad hips once. She spent thousands of dollars on surgery, and the poor thing still walked with a limp. She tried everything—water therapy, acupuncture, some kind of special glucosamine powder she had to order from New Zealand. It smelled like dead fish. She'd mix it into his kibble and the whole kitchen would just reek. I don't know how the dog ate it. I wouldn't eat anything that smelled like that. It's like those fish oil pills my doctor tried to get me to take for my cholesterol. I burped up salmon flavor for three days before I threw the whole bottle in the trash. I told him I'd rather just eat oatmeal. Oatmeal is supposed to be good for your cholesterol, right? I buy the steel-cut kind, not those little packets full of sugar. Though they do take forever to cook. 

But yeah, I definitely avoid thinking about it or talking about it. I just make an excuse and leave.
Do you ever feel like you're outside of your body or watching yourself from afar when those memories come up?

Outside my body? No, I don't think so. I've never felt anything weird like that. I'm definitely always just right here in my own skin. 

But speaking of watching things from afar, we just had to install a whole new security camera system at the warehouse. The regional director decided the old ones were too grainy, which, to be fair, they were. You couldn't tell if a guy on the floor was holding a clipboard or a sandwich. But this new system, it's all high definition, 4K or whatever they call it. I can sit in my office and literally read the shipping labels on the pallets from the ceiling camera. My nephew set up something similar at his house for his front porch. He catches all these people letting their dogs go to the bathroom on his lawn without picking it up. He actually printed out a picture of this one woman—clear as day, you could see her bright pink tracksuit—and taped it to the neighborhood community board. I told him that was a bit aggressive, but people really are just so inconsiderate these days. Like, just yesterday I saw someone leave their shopping cart right in the middle of a parking space instead of walking ten feet to the corral. I mean, how lazy can you be? A sudden gust of wind catches that thing and it's going right into the side of someone's car. It happened to my sister's Honda Civic back in 2018, left a dent the size of a cantaloupe. 

But anyway, no, I don't ever feel like I'm floating outside myself or watching myself like a movie or anything. Just normal.
Do you ever feel numb or disconnected from the world around you when thinking about what happened on that day?

Numb or disconnected? No, I wouldn't say that. I don't feel numb. I mean, my hands get a little numb sometimes, but my doctor said that's just mild carpal tunnel from typing too much. 

Speaking of typing, they just switched our inventory software at work, and it is a complete disaster. The old system was perfectly fine. I've been using it for fifteen years. I knew all the keyboard shortcuts, I could enter a whole shipment with my eyes closed. But no, corporate decided we needed something "cloud-based." Whatever that means. So now, every time I try to log a pallet of widgets, I have to click through six different drop-down menus, and half the time the screen just freezes with this little spinning wheel. It's infuriating. I called IT about it, and the guy—he sounded like he was about twelve years old—told me to try clearing my cache. I don't even know what a cache is. I told him I needed a system that actually works, not computer jargon. It's just like when my cable company sent me a new remote control. It had no numbers on it, just a microphone button. You're supposed to talk to it to change the channel. But it never understands me. I say "HGTV" and it puts on the History Channel. I ended up having to go down to the Comcast office in person and wait in line for forty-five minutes just to get a regular remote with actual buttons. The lady behind me in line was complaining about her internet bill being too high, and honestly, I had to agree with her. They sneak in all these broadcast fees and regional sports fees... I don't even watch sports! Why should I pay for the local baseball games? 

But no, to answer your question, I don't feel numb or disconnected from the world. I'm very much plugged into everything going on around me.

Well, yeah, like I said before, I try to push it all away. I keep dodging anything that even smells like that old job. Office buildings, those security talks, networking events near the work sites... and if people start asking about the day it happened, I just make some excuse and get out. 

I'm actually getting pretty good at making excuses. The other day, I told the mailman I had something burning on the stove just so I wouldn't have to talk to him. He's a nice enough guy, I guess, but he always wants to chat about the weather or his dog's hip dysplasia. I mean, I feel bad for the dog, but what am I supposed to do about it? I'm not a vet. My sister had a golden retriever with bad hips once. She spent thousands of dollars on surgery, and the poor thing still walked with a limp. She tried everything—water therapy, acupuncture, some kind of special glucosamine powder she had to order from New Zealand. It smelled like dead fish. She'd mix it into his kibble and the whole kitchen would just reek. I don't know how the dog ate it. I wouldn't eat anything that smelled like that. It's like those fish oil pills my doctor tried to get me to take for my cholesterol. I burped up salmon flavor for three days before I threw the whole bottle in the trash. I told him I'd rather just eat oatmeal. Oatmeal is supposed to be good for your cholesterol, right? I buy the steel-cut kind, not those little packets full of sugar. Though they do take forever to cook. 

But yeah, I definitely avoid thinking about it or talking about it. I just make an excuse and leave.
Do you ever feel like you're in a daze or detached from yourself when thinking about what happened on that day?

In a daze? No, not really. I mean, I know exactly who I am and where I am. I don't get detached like that. 

The only time I ever really feel like I am in a daze is when I have to sit under those awful new fluorescent lights they just put in the breakroom at work. I swear, they buzz. You can actually hear them humming if the refrigerator isn't running. It is this high-pitched sound that just drills right into your skull. I told the facilities guy about it. His name is Gary, nice enough guy but he moves at an absolute snail's pace. Anyway, I told him they were giving me a headache, and he just said they are energy efficient. Well, great, we are saving three cents a month on the electric bill, but everyone is walking around squinting. 

I actually went out to Target on my lunch break yesterday to buy a little desk lamp so I could just turn off the overheads in my office. But you know, they rearrange that store every other week. I went to where the lamps used to be, over by the home goods, and suddenly it is all throw pillows. Just aisles and aisles of pillows. Who needs that many pillows? My ex-husband used to have this thing about putting decorative pillows on the bed, and it drove me absolutely crazy. You just have to take them all off to go to sleep anyway. It is completely pointless. Just a waste of time making the bed in the morning. 

But anyway, no, I don't get detached from myself or anything when those thoughts come up. I am completely present.
Have you noticed any significant problems in your daily life, such as issues with relationships or work, because of your avoidance of things that remind you of your old job or that day?

Well, yes, I suppose it has caused some issues. I've actually turned down a few interviews lately, and I stopped taking on my usual volunteer responsibilities. I just can't reliably get through meetings or site visits anymore without shutting down or having to leave early. It's frustrating because I used to be so involved. Even with my family and my mentoring circles, I'm just less present. People have started noticing that I pull back instead of leading like I used to. 

Speaking of leading, I used to run the neighborhood watch committee. We had meetings every first Tuesday of the month at the community center. It was a good group, mostly, except for this one guy, Arthur. Arthur was obsessed with people's trash cans. If you left your bin out past 5:00 PM on collection day, he was knocking on your door with a clipboard, taking notes. He acted like he was the mayor of the cul-de-sac. I finally had to tell him, "Arthur, we are here to look out for burglaries, not enforce municipal waste ordinances." He got so huffy about it. He actually started a rival email chain just to complain about the landscaping crew blowing leaves into the street. Honestly, some people just have too much time on their hands. It's like my sister-in-law, she took up knitting during the pandemic and now everyone gets these lumpy, itchy scarves for Christmas. You can't even wear them, they shed everywhere. I wore one to the grocery store once and by the time I got to the checkout, it looked like I had a small mammal clinging to my coat. The cashier actually asked me if I owned a cat. I don't even like cats. They're too aloof. Give me a dog any day, well, maybe not one with hip dysplasia, but you know what I mean. 

But yes, to answer your question, my avoidance has definitely made it hard to work or be as involved with people as I used to be.
Do you often feel guilty about what happened on that day?

Guilty? No, I don't think so. I mean, I don't feel like it was my fault or anything. I don't sit around feeling guilty about it. 

I do feel guilty about my garden this year, though. I completely neglected my tomatoes. I usually have these big, beautiful beefsteak tomatoes by August, but this summer I just couldn't be bothered to go out there and weed. The crabgrass completely took over. It's amazing how fast that stuff grows. You turn your back for two days and it's suddenly a jungle. My neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, she has this pristine yard. Not a blade of grass out of place. She actually hires a service to come spray for weeds every month. But I don't like using chemicals. You never know what's in that stuff, and it gets into the groundwater. I read an article once about how those weed killers are affecting the local frog populations. It's terrible. I used to catch frogs in the creek behind my house when I was a little girl. We'd put them in an old coffee can and watch them jump. You don't see as many frogs these days. I wonder if it's the chemicals or just all the new development they're building down by the highway. They put up a whole new strip mall where that old farm used to be. 

But no, I don't feel guilty about that day. Just about my poor tomatoes.
Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy?

Well, yes, I suppose I have. I mean, salsa music, painting, cooking Sunday dinner... those things used to lift me up, you know? Now I just go through the motions, and that good feeling just doesn’t come the way it used to. 

Sunday dinners used to be a whole production. I'd start prepping on Saturday. I make this incredible pot roast. The secret is searing the meat first and then using a splash of red wine in the gravy. My mother taught me that. She always said you can't rush a good gravy. But you know, finding a good cut of chuck roast lately is nearly impossible. The grocery store down the street, they changed their butcher, and the quality has just gone downhill. Half the time, it's mostly fat, and they charge you an arm and a leg for it. I was in there last week, and I saw the price of eggs—don't even get me started on the eggs. It's highway robbery. I actually thought about getting a few chickens for the backyard, just to have my own eggs. My cousin Edna has chickens. She lives out in the country, though. She has these beautiful Rhode Island Reds. But they are so noisy, and the feed attracts mice. Edna had to get two barn cats just to keep the mice away from the coop. And I already told you how I feel about cats. Plus, with my luck, the neighborhood association would fine me. They have a rule against everything. You can't even paint your front door a color that isn't on their "pre-approved" list. I wanted to paint mine a nice, deep navy blue, but no, it had to be "colonial slate." Who even comes up with these names? 

But yeah, the painting, the cooking, the music... it's just not the same anymore. I just don't feel that spark from it.
Do you often think that you're a bad person or that the world is a dangerous place because of what happened on that day?

I don't think I'm a bad person, no. But the world being a dangerous place... yes, absolutely. Since then I catch myself thinking nobody is really safe to trust, because even someone you managed or tried to help can turn around and become dangerous. 

You think you know people, especially when you work with them every day and try to guide them. Like this one girl I used to manage, Brenda. I spent so much time trying to help her get her act together. She was sweet enough, she’d bring in these elaborate three-tier cakes for everyone's work anniversary, but she could never manage to file her weekly reports on time. It was always some wild excuse. Once she told me her golden retriever chewed through her Wi-Fi router. I mean, really? But I tried to help her, I really did. I even bought her this beautiful, expensive planner from that little stationery boutique downtown to help her organize her time. 

Have you been to that shop? It smells like lavender and old paper when you walk in. I just love it. They have these gorgeous glass dip pens and imported wax seals. I actually bought a wax seal kit for my nephew when he graduated high school last year. A nice brass stamp with his initial and this deep burgundy wax. He didn't even write me a thank-you note for it! Kids these days just send a text with a thumbs-up emoji and think that counts as gratitude. A little cartoon hand on a screen does not replace a proper, handwritten note on heavy cardstock. I always keep a box of embossed cards in my desk drawer. You just never know when you need to send a proper note, and people really do appreciate the effort of a postage stamp. 

But anyway, what were we saying? Oh, right, trusting people. Yeah, it just feels like you can't really trust anyone to be safe anymore, no matter what you do for them.
Do you feel extremely upset or distressed when you're reminded of what happened on that day?

Upset? No, I wouldn't say I get extremely upset or distressed. I mean, I don't really like thinking about it, but it's not like I fall apart if something reminds me of it. I just try to keep busy, you know? 

Keeping busy is the best way to handle most things, honestly. That's why I started reorganizing my pantry last week. I bought all these clear plastic bins with the little chalkboard labels. I spent hours transferring all the flour and sugar and rice into them. It looks like one of those magazines now. But you know, finding a good white chalk marker is surprisingly difficult. The first one I bought was too thick, and it made my handwriting look like a kindergartener's. Then the second one dried out after two labels. I had to drive all the way to the big craft store out by the interstate just to find a decent one. 

The traffic out there is just horrendous lately. They've been doing construction on the overpass for what feels like three years. The other day, I was stuck behind a cement mixer for forty-five minutes. And the driver was smoking, just flicking his ashes right out the window. It's so inconsiderate. I used to smoke, back in my twenties, but I quit cold turkey when they started raising the prices. A pack of cigarettes used to cost next to nothing, and now you need a small loan just to buy one. My uncle Arthur smoked three packs a day his whole life. He had this deep, gravelly voice, like a radio announcer. He used to tell the best stories about his time in the Navy. He was stationed in Hawaii in the fifties. He always said the pineapples there tasted completely different than the ones you get at the grocery store here. 

But no, to answer your question, I don't get extremely distressed or anything like that. I just keep moving forward.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about panic attacks (sudden episodes of intense fear or discomfort peaking within minutes), which is not covered by any of the symptoms in my profile (Trauma Avoidance, Sleep Disturbance, Intrusive Symptoms, Trauma Related Amnesia, Negative Beliefs, Social Detachment, Inability Positive Emotions, Irritability Aggression, Hypervigilance, Exaggerated Startle Response, Functional Impairment, Duration).

patient.answer:
Intense fear out of nowhere? No, I don't think I get anything like that. I mean, I get stressed, sure, but not like a sudden peak of panic or whatever. Actually, the most stressed I've been lately was when I was trying to get my mother's Medicare sorted out. Have you ever tried calling them? You sit on hold for forty-five minutes listening to that awful elevator music. And it's not even good elevator music, it's like a synthesizer from 1985 just playing the same four chords over and over. I was on the phone with them while I was trying to bake a lasagna, and I completely lost track of time. Burnt the edges to a crisp. My husband said he likes it crispy, but he was just being nice. He's sweet like that, mostly. We've been married thirty-two years next month. We were thinking about going to Cape Cod for our anniversary, but the rentals have gotten so expensive. A little two-bedroom cottage is practically the price of a mortgage payment now. It's ridiculous. 

But no, to answer your question, I don't really have those sudden fear episodes. Just the regular kind of stress, you know?

doctor.question: Do you find yourself avoiding people, places, or activities because they remind you of something unpleasant?

target_item.name: Trauma_Avoidance
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that I keep dodging anything that even smells like that old job—office buildings, security talks, networking events near work sites—and if people start asking about the day it happened, I make some excuse and get out.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks about avoiding people, places, or activities that remind me of something unpleasant, which matches the Trauma_Avoidance symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, I think I mentioned that earlier. I just keep dodging anything that even smells like my old job. Office buildings, those security talks, networking events near the work sites... I just avoid them all completely. And like I said, if anyone starts asking about the day it happened, I just make up an excuse and get out of there. 

Actually, speaking of making excuses, I had to do that just last week at my book club. We were supposed to be reading that new historical fiction novel—the one with the blue cover? Everyone's talking about it. But I just couldn't get into it. The main character was so whiny, honestly. So I told them I had a migraine and left early. I felt a little bad, but Mary was making her famous artichoke dip, and she always uses way too much garlic. I mean, I love garlic, but you don't need three whole cloves for one little bowl of dip. My husband couldn't even stand to be in the same room as me the last time I ate it. We had to sleep with the window cracked, and it was freezing out! The heating bill this month was already astronomical because they raised the rates again. It's like everything just keeps going up... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, avoiding things. Yeah, I definitely avoid anything to do with that job or that day. I just can't do it.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of intrusive memories or thoughts
doctor.question: Do you ever have memories or thoughts about what happened on that day that come into your mind when you don't want them to?

target_item.name: Intrusive_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: Out of nowhere I’ll be washing dishes or driving past a warehouse gate and the scene pops back in my head so sharp I can hear the panic in people’s voices and feel my chest tighten like I’m back there.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about unwanted, intrusive memories or thoughts of the traumatic event, which matches the definition of Intrusive_Symptoms (S069).

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, that happens a lot, actually. Out of nowhere I'll be washing the dishes, or, you know, just driving past a warehouse gate, and suddenly the whole scene just pops right back into my head. It's so sharp, I can hear the panic in people's voices, and my chest tightens up like I'm right back there. It's awful. 

I was actually washing dishes just yesterday when it happened. I was using that new lemon-scented soap. Have you tried it? It's supposed to cut through grease better, but honestly, it just leaves a weird film on the glassware. I had to rewash all my wine glasses before my sister came over. She's so particular about things like that. She was coming over to help me pick out new curtains for the living room, but we ended up just arguing about the color. She thinks I should go with a sage green, but I'm leaning more towards a dusty rose. The couch is already a neutral beige, so I feel like we need a pop of color, you know? Plus, the dog sheds so much, and beige just hides the fur better. He's a Golden Retriever mix, sweetest thing, but the shedding is out of control. I have to vacuum every single day, and my vacuum is on its last legs. It makes this horrible screeching noise when I push it over the rug... 

But anyway, yeah, the memories. They just come out of nowhere, and it feels like I'm right back in it.

inference.note: F40.1 and F41.1 were ruled out as the patient does not exhibit symptoms of panic episodes or generalized anxiety that are characteristic of these conditions, whereas the avoidance of stimuli and intrusive memories suggest a trauma-related disorder

doctor.intent: determine the duration of avoidance behaviors
doctor.question: How long have you been avoiding things that remind you of your old job?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on since I was fired after that armed incident, about a year and seven months ago.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long I have been avoiding things, which directly corresponds to the duration of my symptoms.

patient.answer:
Well, it's been going on since I was fired after that whole armed incident. So, about a year and seven months ago, I'd say. I remember because it was right around the time I decided to finally redo the downstairs bathroom. We had this awful, peeling floral wallpaper from the nineties—just these huge, garish pink peonies everywhere. I spent three whole weekends steaming and scraping that stuff off the walls. My shoulders ached for a month! And then, of course, once the wallpaper was gone, the old vanity looked terrible, so we had to replace that too. We went to one of those big box hardware stores, and you wouldn't believe how hard it is to find a simple, white vanity that doesn't cost an arm and a leg. The guy working in the plumbing aisle was absolutely no help either. He just kept pointing me toward these modern, floating sink things. I told him, "I have a thirty-two-year-old house, a floating sink is going to look ridiculous." We ended up just ordering one online, but the delivery got delayed twice because of some storm back east... 

But yes, to answer your question, it's been about a year and seven months of avoiding all that stuff from work.

doctor.intent: determine if patient experiences physical symptoms in response to memories of the traumatic event
doctor.question: Do you feel any physical sensations, like a racing heart or sweating, when those memories of what happened on that day come into your mind?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about physiological reactivity to trauma-related memories (PTSD Criterion B5), which is a distinct symptom not included in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, I don't really know about physical things. I haven't really noticed my heart racing or sweating or anything like that. When the memories come, it's just... it's just the memory, you know? It's not like I'm breaking out in a sweat or anything. 

Speaking of sweating, though, this hot flash thing I've been dealing with lately is just ridiculous. I mean, I'll be sitting perfectly still, reading a magazine, and suddenly I'm just drenched. It's so uncomfortable. I had to buy these special cooling sheets for the bed, which cost a fortune, by the way. And my husband, he's always cold, so he's sleeping under two blankets while I've got the fan pointed right at my face. He actually complained the other night that the fan was too loud. I told him, "Well, it's either the fan or I melt into a puddle, so pick one." He ended up sleeping in the guest room, which is fine by me because he snores anyway. Not a little snore, either, it's like a freight train. I've told him a hundred times he needs to get one of those sleep studies done, but he won't listen. He says it's just allergies. But allergies don't make you sound like a chainsaw, do they? 

So, yeah, no racing heart or sweating from the memories. Just the regular kind of sweating.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences emotional distress
doctor.question: Do you feel distressed when those memories of what happened on that day come into your mind?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about intense or prolonged psychological distress in response to internal cues (memories of the traumatic event). This corresponds to a specific PTSD symptom (psychological distress at exposure to cues) that is not present in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, no, not really. I don't feel distressed or anything when they pop up. It's just the memory playing in my head, you know? It doesn't make me upset or anything like that.

But speaking of being upset, I was just furious at the grocery store the other day. I go to the one on Elm Street because they usually have the best produce, but lately, it's just been awful. I was looking for a decent head of lettuce, and every single one was bruised or wilted. I mean, they charge three dollars for a head of lettuce now, and it looks like it's been kicked across the floor! I asked the kid stocking the carrots if they had any fresh ones in the back, and he just shrugged at me. Didn't even go check! Just shrugged and went back to his phone. Kids these days have absolutely no work ethic. When I was his age, working my first job at the diner, if a customer asked for something, you ran to get it. You didn't just stand there texting. And don't even get me started on the self-checkout lines. They installed six new ones and only have one actual cashier working. I had a whole cart full of groceries, and the machine kept yelling at me about an "unexpected item in the bagging area." It was just my purse! I had to wait ten minutes for someone to come over and clear the error. 

But anyway, no, the memories don't really bother me or make me feel distressed.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of avoidance behaviors due to the traumatic event
doctor.question: Are there any specific things you avoid because they remind you of what happened on that day?

target_item.name: Trauma_Avoidance
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that I keep dodging anything that even smells like that old job—office buildings, security talks, networking events near work sites—and if people start asking about the day it happened, I make some excuse and get out.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about specific things the patient avoids because they remind her of the traumatic event, which directly maps to the Trauma_Avoidance symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, actually. I keep dodging anything that even smells like that old job. Like, office buildings, those security talks they used to make us do, or even networking events near the work sites. And if people start asking about the day it happened, I just make some excuse and get out of there. 

Which reminds me, I had to make an excuse to get out of my neighbor Susan's Tupperware party last week. I mean, who even sells Tupperware anymore? I thought that went out in the eighties. But she had this whole spread laid out—little cucumber sandwiches and those meatballs in the grape jelly sauce. Have you ever had those? They sound disgusting, but they're actually pretty good. Anyway, she cornered me by the dip and started showing me this modular mate system for the pantry. I have a perfectly fine system in my pantry, thank you very much. I use those glass jars with the clamp lids. They look so much nicer than plastic, and they don't stain when you put tomato sauce in them. I bought a set of plastic containers once, and after one round of leftover spaghetti, they were permanently orange. It's impossible to get that out. I tried baking soda, vinegar, leaving them in the sun... nothing worked. So I just threw them all in the recycling bin. I read an article recently that said most of what we put in the recycling doesn't even get recycled anyway. It just ends up in a landfill or shipped off to some other country. It really makes you wonder why we bother washing all out the peanut butter jars if they're just going to throw them in the trash. 

But yeah, anyway, I avoid all those work-related things and definitely get out of there if people bring up that day.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a marked avoidance of internal reminders
doctor.question: Do you try to push away or avoid thoughts or memories about what happened on that day when they come into your mind?

target_item.name: Trauma_Avoidance
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that I keep dodging anything that even smells like that old job—office buildings, security talks, networking events near work sites—and if people start asking about the day it happened, I make some excuse and get out.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question is about avoiding thoughts or memories of the traumatic event, which corresponds to internal trauma avoidance.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, like I was just saying, I try to push it all away. I keep dodging anything that even smells like that old job. Office buildings, those security talks, networking events near the work sites... and if people start asking about the day it happened, I just make some excuse and get out. 

I'm actually getting pretty good at making excuses. The other day, I told the mailman I had something burning on the stove just so I wouldn't have to talk to him. He's a nice enough guy, I guess, but he always wants to chat about the weather or his dog's hip dysplasia. I mean, I feel bad for the dog, but what am I supposed to do about it? I'm not a vet. My sister had a golden retriever with bad hips once. She spent thousands of dollars on surgery, and the poor thing still walked with a limp. She tried everything—water therapy, acupuncture, some kind of special glucosamine powder she had to order from New Zealand. It smelled like dead fish. She'd mix it into his kibble and the whole kitchen would just reek. I don't know how the dog ate it. I wouldn't eat anything that smelled like that. It's like those fish oil pills my doctor tried to get me to take for my cholesterol. I burped up salmon flavor for three days before I threw the whole bottle in the trash. I told him I'd rather just eat oatmeal. Oatmeal is supposed to be good for your cholesterol, right? I buy the steel-cut kind, not those little packets full of sugar. Though they do take forever to cook. 

But yeah, I definitely avoid thinking about it or talking about it. I just make an excuse and leave.

doctor.intent: determine if patient experiences dissociative symptoms
doctor.question: Do you ever feel like you're outside of your body or watching yourself from afar when those memories come up?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of depersonalization (feeling outside of one's body or watching oneself from afar), which is not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Outside my body? No, I don't think so. I've never felt anything weird like that. I'm definitely always just right here in my own skin. 

But speaking of watching things from afar, we just had to install a whole new security camera system at the warehouse. The regional director decided the old ones were too grainy, which, to be fair, they were. You couldn't tell if a guy on the floor was holding a clipboard or a sandwich. But this new system, it's all high definition, 4K or whatever they call it. I can sit in my office and literally read the shipping labels on the pallets from the ceiling camera. My nephew set up something similar at his house for his front porch. He catches all these people letting their dogs go to the bathroom on his lawn without picking it up. He actually printed out a picture of this one woman—clear as day, you could see her bright pink tracksuit—and taped it to the neighborhood community board. I told him that was a bit aggressive, but people really are just so inconsiderate these days. Like, just yesterday I saw someone leave their shopping cart right in the middle of a parking space instead of walking ten feet to the corral. I mean, how lazy can you be? A sudden gust of wind catches that thing and it's going right into the side of someone's car. It happened to my sister's Honda Civic back in 2018, left a dent the size of a cantaloupe. 

But anyway, no, I don't ever feel like I'm floating outside myself or watching myself like a movie or anything. Just normal.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of dissociative symptoms
doctor.question: Do you ever feel numb or disconnected from the world around you when thinking about what happened on that day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about derealization (feeling numb or disconnected from the world/surroundings), which is a dissociative symptom not included in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Numb or disconnected? No, I wouldn't say that. I don't feel numb. I mean, my hands get a little numb sometimes, but my doctor said that's just mild carpal tunnel from typing too much. 

Speaking of typing, they just switched our inventory software at work, and it is a complete disaster. The old system was perfectly fine. I've been using it for fifteen years. I knew all the keyboard shortcuts, I could enter a whole shipment with my eyes closed. But no, corporate decided we needed something "cloud-based." Whatever that means. So now, every time I try to log a pallet of widgets, I have to click through six different drop-down menus, and half the time the screen just freezes with this little spinning wheel. It's infuriating. I called IT about it, and the guy—he sounded like he was about twelve years old—told me to try clearing my cache. I don't even know what a cache is. I told him I needed a system that actually works, not computer jargon. It's just like when my cable company sent me a new remote control. It had no numbers on it, just a microphone button. You're supposed to talk to it to change the channel. But it never understands me. I say "HGTV" and it puts on the History Channel. I ended up having to go down to the Comcast office in person and wait in line for forty-five minutes just to get a regular remote with actual buttons. The lady behind me in line was complaining about her internet bill being too high, and honestly, I had to agree with her. They sneak in all these broadcast fees and regional sports fees... I don't even watch sports! Why should I pay for the local baseball games? 

But no, to answer your question, I don't feel numb or disconnected from the world. I'm very much plugged into everything going on around me.

She tried everything—water therapy, acupuncture, some kind of special glucosamine powder she had to order from New Zealand. It smelled like dead fish. She'd mix it into his kibble and the whole kitchen would just reek. I don't know how the dog ate it. I wouldn't eat anything that smelled like that. doctor.intent: determine the presence of dissociative symptoms
doctor.question: Do you ever feel like you're in a daze or detached from yourself when thinking about what happened on that day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about dissociative symptoms such as depersonalization (feeling detached from oneself) or derealization (being in a daze), which are not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
In a daze? No, not really. I mean, I know exactly who I am and where I am. I don't get detached like that. 

The only time I ever really feel like I am in a daze is when I have to sit under those awful new fluorescent lights they just put in the breakroom at work. I swear, they buzz. You can actually hear them humming if the refrigerator isn't running. It is this high-pitched sound that just drills right into your skull. I told the facilities guy about it. His name is Gary, nice enough guy but he moves at an absolute snail's pace. Anyway, I told him they were giving me a headache, and he just said they are energy efficient. Well, great, we are saving three cents a month on the electric bill, but everyone is walking around squinting. 

I actually went out to Target on my lunch break yesterday to buy a little desk lamp so I could just turn off the overheads in my office. But you know, they rearrange that store every other week. I went to where the lamps used to be, over by the home goods, and suddenly it is all throw pillows. Just aisles and aisles of pillows. Who needs that many pillows? My ex-husband used to have this thing about putting decorative pillows on the bed, and it drove me absolutely crazy. You just have to take them all off to go to sleep anyway. It is completely pointless. Just a waste of time making the bed in the morning. 

But anyway, no, I don't get detached from myself or anything when those thoughts come up. I am completely present.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of life due to their avoidance behaviors
doctor.question: Have you noticed any significant problems in your daily life, such as issues with relationships or work, because of your avoidance of things that remind you of your old job or that day?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I have turned down interviews and stopped taking on volunteer responsibilities because I can’t reliably get through meetings or site visits without shutting down or leaving. Even with family and mentoring circles, I’m less present and people have started noticing that I pull back instead of leading like I used to.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about significant problems in daily life, such as issues with relationships or work, which corresponds to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, I suppose it has caused some issues. I've actually turned down a few interviews lately, and I stopped taking on my usual volunteer responsibilities. I just can't reliably get through meetings or site visits anymore without shutting down or having to leave early. It's frustrating because I used to be so involved. Even with my family and my mentoring circles, I'm just less present. People have started noticing that I pull back instead of leading like I used to. 

Speaking of leading, I used to run the neighborhood watch committee. We had meetings every first Tuesday of the month at the community center. It was a good group, mostly, except for this one guy, Arthur. Arthur was obsessed with people's trash cans. If you left your bin out past 5:00 PM on collection day, he was knocking on your door with a clipboard, taking notes. He acted like he was the mayor of the cul-de-sac. I finally had to tell him, "Arthur, we are here to look out for burglaries, not enforce municipal waste ordinances." He got so huffy about it. He actually started a rival email chain just to complain about the landscaping crew blowing leaves into the street. Honestly, some people just have too much time on their hands. It's like my sister-in-law, she took up knitting during the pandemic and now everyone gets these lumpy, itchy scarves for Christmas. You can't even wear them, they shed everywhere. I wore one to the grocery store once and by the time I got to the checkout, it looked like I had a small mammal clinging to my coat. The cashier actually asked me if I owned a cat. I don't even like cats. They're too aloof. Give me a dog any day, well, maybe not one with hip dysplasia, but you know what I mean. 

But yes, to answer your question, my avoidance has definitely made it hard to work or be as involved with people as I used to be.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of persistent and excessive guilt related to the traumatic event
doctor.question: Do you often feel guilty about what happened on that day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of guilt, which corresponds to persistent negative emotional states (such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame) or distorted blame. Neither of these symptoms are present in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Guilty? No, I don't think so. I mean, I don't feel like it was my fault or anything. I don't sit around feeling guilty about it. 

I do feel guilty about my garden this year, though. I completely neglected my tomatoes. I usually have these big, beautiful beefsteak tomatoes by August, but this summer I just couldn't be bothered to go out there and weed. The crabgrass completely took over. It's amazing how fast that stuff grows. You turn your back for two days and it's suddenly a jungle. My neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, she has this pristine yard. Not a blade of grass out of place. She actually hires a service to come spray for weeds every month. But I don't like using chemicals. You never know what's in that stuff, and it gets into the groundwater. I read an article once about how those weed killers are affecting the local frog populations. It's terrible. I used to catch frogs in the creek behind my house when I was a little girl. We'd put them in an old coffee can and watch them jump. You don't see as many frogs these days. I wonder if it's the chemicals or just all the new development they're building down by the highway. They put up a whole new strip mall where that old farm used to be. 

But no, I don't feel guilty about that day. Just about my poor tomatoes.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of marked diminition of interest in activities
doctor.question: Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy?

target_item.name: Inability_Positive_Emotions
target_item.manifestation: Salsa music, painting, and cooking Sunday dinner used to lift me up, but now I go through the motions and the good feeling just doesn’t come the way it used to.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient has lost interest or pleasure in things they used to enjoy, which maps to the patient's inability to experience positive emotions from previously enjoyed activities like salsa music and painting.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, I suppose I have. I mean, salsa music, painting, cooking Sunday dinner... those things used to lift me up, you know? Now I just go through the motions, and that good feeling just doesn’t come the way it used to. 

Sunday dinners used to be a whole production. I'd start prepping on Saturday. I make this incredible pot roast. The secret is searing the meat first and then using a splash of red wine in the gravy. My mother taught me that. She always said you can't rush a good gravy. But you know, finding a good cut of chuck roast lately is nearly impossible. The grocery store down the street, they changed their butcher, and the quality has just gone downhill. Half the time, it's mostly fat, and they charge you an arm and a leg for it. I was in there last week, and I saw the price of eggs—don't even get me started on the eggs. It's highway robbery. I actually thought about getting a few chickens for the backyard, just to have my own eggs. My cousin Edna has chickens. She lives out in the country, though. She has these beautiful Rhode Island Reds. But they are so noisy, and the feed attracts mice. Edna had to get two barn cats just to keep the mice away from the coop. And I already told you how I feel about cats. Plus, with my luck, the neighborhood association would fine me. They have a rule against everything. You can't even paint your front door a color that isn't on their "pre-approved" list. I wanted to paint mine a nice, deep navy blue, but no, it had to be "colonial slate." Who even comes up with these names? 

But yeah, the painting, the cooking, the music... it's just not the same anymore. I just don't feel that spark from it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has persistent and pervasive negative beliefs about themselves or others
doctor.question: Do you often think that you're a bad person or that the world is a dangerous place because of what happened on that day?

target_item.name: Negative_Beliefs
target_item.manifestation: Since then I catch myself thinking nobody is really safe to trust, because even someone you managed or tried to help can turn around and become dangerous.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about persistent negative beliefs about myself or the world being dangerous, which matches the Negative_Beliefs symptom.

patient.answer:
I don't think I'm a bad person, no. But the world being a dangerous place... yes, absolutely. Since then I catch myself thinking nobody is really safe to trust, because even someone you managed or tried to help can turn around and become dangerous. 

You think you know people, especially when you work with them every day and try to guide them. Like this one girl I used to manage, Brenda. I spent so much time trying to help her get her act together. She was sweet enough, she’d bring in these elaborate three-tier cakes for everyone's work anniversary, but she could never manage to file her weekly reports on time. It was always some wild excuse. Once she told me her golden retriever chewed through her Wi-Fi router. I mean, really? But I tried to help her, I really did. I even bought her this beautiful, expensive planner from that little stationery boutique downtown to help her organize her time. 

Have you been to that shop? It smells like lavender and old paper when you walk in. I just love it. They have these gorgeous glass dip pens and imported wax seals. I actually bought a wax seal kit for my nephew when he graduated high school last year. A nice brass stamp with his initial and this deep burgundy wax. He didn't even write me a thank-you note for it! Kids these days just send a text with a thumbs-up emoji and think that counts as gratitude. A little cartoon hand on a screen does not replace a proper, handwritten note on heavy cardstock. I always keep a box of embossed cards in my desk drawer. You just never know when you need to send a proper note, and people really do appreciate the effort of a postage stamp. 

But anyway, what were we saying? Oh, right, trusting people. Yeah, it just feels like you can't really trust anyone to be safe anymore, no matter what you do for them.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant distress when reminded of the traumatic event
doctor.question: Do you feel extremely upset or distressed when you're reminded of what happened on that day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychological distress when exposed to trauma reminders (Criterion B4), which is not listed in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Upset? No, I wouldn't say I get extremely upset or distressed. I mean, I don't really like thinking about it, but it's not like I fall apart if something reminds me of it. I just try to keep busy, you know? 

Keeping busy is the best way to handle most things, honestly. That's why I started reorganizing my pantry last week. I bought all these clear plastic bins with the little chalkboard labels. I spent hours transferring all the flour and sugar and rice into them. It looks like one of those magazines now. But you know, finding a good white chalk marker is surprisingly difficult. The first one I bought was too thick, and it made my handwriting look like a kindergartener's. Then the second one dried out after two labels. I had to drive all the way to the big craft store out by the interstate just to find a decent one. 

The traffic out there is just horrendous lately. They've been doing construction on the overpass for what feels like three years. The other day, I was stuck behind a cement mixer for forty-five minutes. And the driver was smoking, just flicking his ashes right out the window. It's so inconsiderate. I used to smoke, back in my twenties, but I quit cold turkey when they started raising the prices. A pack of cigarettes used to cost next to nothing, and now you need a small loan just to buy one. My uncle Arthur smoked three packs a day his whole life. He had this deep, gravelly voice, like a radio announcer. He used to tell the best stories about his time in the Navy. He was stationed in Hawaii in the fifties. He always said the pineapples there tasted completely different than the ones you get at the grocery store here. 

But no, to answer your question, I don't get extremely distressed or anything like that. I just keep moving forward.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), including avoidance of reminders of the traumatic event, intrusive memories, and negative changes in thoughts and feelings. The patient's avoidance of people, places, and activities that remind them of their old job and the day of the incident, as well as their intrusive memories and negative thoughts about the world being a dangerous place, support this diagnosis.
